# Independent audit: transformed component mesh recovery



## Block normalization and actual fine measure

An orthogonal postcomposition can send the image of the original continuous s-subspace back to that subspace. Thus every unconstrained invertible shape normalization can be replaced by the stated block map `(u,x)->(Au,Bu+Cx)` without changing its determinant or diameter bounds. Preservation of the s-subspace forces the upper-right block to vanish, and invertibility gives invertible A and C. At s=0 the condition is vacuous and det C=1.

The representation-affine positional corrections are applied after these maps and preserve all anchored component relations. Their first r coordinates translate the actual residual fine coset to

    A_(l,i)(Lambda_l+a_l)-g_(l,z),u.

The offsets may vary with z. They do not change the lattice covering radius or covolume. The residual fine covolume is `v_l |det A_(l,i)|`; the s-dimensional Jacobian on a fixed original fine section is `|det C_(l,i)|`. Their product is exactly v_l/M_l, independent of component. Hence the global affine source map pushes the auxiliary weighted fine measure to mu_l/M_l, including total mass. Orthogonal embedding into a component block contributes no additional Jacobian.

There is no implicit assertion of a common unweighted fine lattice in the lift. The variable-covolume measure sigma_l is used only in direct discrepancy estimates and exact affine pullbacks; OC is applied only to the compact intrinsic coarse lift when explicitly assumed later.

The added Section 2.1 also passes. If two translated images of the same anchor contain balls of radii rho and rho_tilde and lie in balls of radii R and R_tilde, their comparison map S sends the first inner ball to an ellipsoid whose diameter is at most 2R_tilde. Hence ||S||<=R_tilde/rho, and the inverse bound follows identically. Both maps preserve the continuous subspace, so the fine block of S is A_tilde A^(-1), with operator norm at most ||S||; the inverse fine block has the analogous bound. Applying these maps to nearest-lattice-point displacements gives exactly the stated two-sided covering-radius comparison. All translation centers are irrelevant to this diameter/width argument. Thus mesh vanishing is invariant among uniformly round block frames of the same anchor, as claimed.

## Uniform residual discrepancy and deterministic center recovery

Covering radius rho_(l,i) gives a measurable Voronoi cell contained in the radius-rho cube for every translated residual coset. All residual bodies occupy a common bounded m-dimensional ball. Therefore the elementary all-convex-set discrepancy applies with error `2r rho_(l,i)(2R+2rho_(l,i))^(m-1)` on each residual fiber, uniformly for every lifted halfspace restriction. Such restrictions may also be empty or entire; those cases satisfy the same bound. Closed supporting fibers and lower-dimensional cuts are retained.

Summing the finite errors gives e_l tending to zero. The coarse lift has total mass one, so the sampled total tends to one and the normalized cap discrepancy is at most 2e_l/(1-e_l). This proves eventual positivity of the actual original fine mass and its asymptotic equality with M_l. It does not assert total variation between sampled and coarse laws.

A limit center can be perturbed inside its own full m-dimensional residual fiber using the already proved component-isolation Lipschitz bound. A fixed neighborhood of that residual point persists in every sufficiently late fiber. Rounding only its residual U coordinates to a nearest point of the actual translated residual coset moves it by at most rho_(l,i); its X coordinates stay fixed. The resulting point is feasible in the residual body and therefore maps to a feasible point of the ORIGINAL fine set.

No bound on the inverse map is required: original x coordinates may change greatly, but membership follows from exact residual membership and the block inverse. Residual total variation, component Lipschitz continuity, and the uniform sampled cap estimate give the desired depth lower bound at this same point. Pullback of every original containing closed halfspace preserves normalized mass exactly and gives the final pointwise inequality. Pure-base or constant restrictions are included; a containing constant restriction is the entire source.

The limiting body is defined after the full-shape subsequence, as stated. The recovery assertion is made along that subsequence and does not identify unrelated subsequential limits.

## Omitted coarse fibers and conditional dimensions

After retaining positive coarse weights, the maps are normalized by M_(l,+), and the retained fine mass tends to that coarse mass. The exact comparison with the full original fine depth has factor

    mu_(l,+)(total)/mu_l(total).

Thus negligible omitted fine mass relative to M_(l,+) is sufficient, while zero omitted coarse weight alone is not. The stated more general factor `1/(1+R_0)` follows from the limsup bound on the omitted fine-to-retained-coarse mass ratio.

The segment warning has omitted sampled mass 2h and zero omitted coarse area, compared with retained coarse area 2h^2. Its retained component can still have transformed mesh tending to zero. This directly certifies the need for a separate fine-mass hypothesis. All its vertices are sampled on the stated reciprocal grids, and its hull contains the fixed full tetrahedron.

The conditional OC application uses the enlarged continuous ambient dimension D, including intrinsic m-dimensional intersections, with D bounded by B(k,m). A deficient retained coarse rank is reduced by the saturated integer lattice map, which leaves the fine coordinates unchanged. The strict constant comparison for s>=1 or for s=0,r>=2 is valid; the excluded s=0,r=1 case is not recovered from that strict comparison alone. At k=0 ordinary full-m-dimensional Grünbaum is the only coarse input.

## Exact example separating the two mesh hypotheses

For h=L^(-2), epsilon=h^2, and a=L^(-1), both endpoint triangles have area 2epsilon. Their sampled vertices lie in hZ. The second triangle’s block map sends its vertices to `(-1/2,0),(1/2,0),(0,1)`, while the first becomes the other stated fixed area-1/2 triangle. Both determinants are 1/(4epsilon), the common 1/M_l.

The transformed spacings are h and h/(2a)=1/(2L), so all retained component meshes vanish. The original Voronoi radius is h/2 and its ratio to total coarse area is L^2/8, tending to infinity. The baseline tetrahedron is the continuous shear of the fixed crossed tetrahedron with shear parameter a tending to zero; its inner and outer radii are uniformly controlled. This geometric shear is not applied to the actual fine lattice.

The second triangle’s exact tent sum is L, giving sampled weighted mass 2epsilon. The first has mass epsilon(2+h), so both normalized component masses tend to one half. Uniform sampling in their fixed triangles gives individual maximum depths tending to 4/9. Each coarse endpoint component can be isolated by an integer tilt, so the combined original fine maximum tends to 2/9. In the separately archived a=h example, the second transformed mesh stays non-dense and the maximum tends to 1/4 instead. These assertions have different hypotheses and do not conflict.

No mathematical gap, missing measure factor, or unsupported discarded-mass passage was found.
